There is a particular kind of magic in the concept of the "Threshold"—the spaces in between. 

We spend almost all of our lives measuring things. We measure time in seconds and years, distance in miles, our lives in milestones achieved or missed. We categorize the world into neat binaries: here and there, day and night, past and future. 

But the most profound experiences rarely happen at the destinations. They happen in the liminal spaces. 

Think of the hypnagogic state—that brief, deeply strange twilight between wakefulness and sleep, where your thoughts unhinge from logic and float freely. Or consider the exact moment of dusk, when the sky isn't yet purple, but the blue has deepened into something mysterious. The light turns molten, shadows stretch, and for about ten minutes, the entire world feels like a held breath. 

Myths and folklore have always understood the power of these in-between spaces. Crossroads are where deals are made with devils, or where travelers must choose their fate. Dusk and dawn are the witching hours, the thresholds where the veil between the physical world and the spiritual world wears thin. Doorways, bridges, and shorelines are all places of transition. They are neither one thing nor the other. 

There is a strange, reckless peace to be found in the middle of a journey. When you are on a train, or flying at 35,000 feet, you are effectively nowhere. You have left, but you have not arrived. All the anxieties of your origin and the expectations of your destination are temporarily suspended. You are simply existing in the transit. You are a passenger in the void.

We are always rushing to cross these thresholds, desperate to get to the other side. We want to get through the workout to get to the shower. We want to get through Friday to get to the weekend. We want to get through the hard year to get to the good one. 

But the threshold has its own weight. It is a place of transformation. A door is useless if you only stand on one side of it; it is the act of crossing that holds the meaning. The next time you find yourself in the middle of a commute, waiting in a hallway, or watching the sun melt into the horizon, try not to rush through it. Stop, and exist exactly in the middle of nowhere. 

It’s a beautiful place to be.
